children: Flock Safety told the U.S. Senate that it has tightened the requirements for police officers and other users to access and search its database of billions of license plates amid growing concerns about misuse of its divisive product.

The Atlanta-based company has made changes to the information users provide when explaining their searches, Flock's chief legal officer said in a letter to Sen. Josh Hawley, a Republican from Missouri. While users have always been required to justify their searches of the company's database, which it said scans 20 billion plates a month, the information was entered "in a free-text field," yielding answers that weren't always specific, the company said in the letter viewed by The Wall Street Journal.

Flock has now added a drop-down menu with standardized categories modeled after the Federal Bureau of Investigation's data-reporting system. Law-enforcement searches will require a case number in order to conduct a search by the end of the year, although the system can be bypassed in an emergency, Flock said.
Hawley launched an investigation into Flock last month and is leading a Wednesday hearing into the company and three competitors that provide similar surveillance systems.

"We have an entire constitutional system to protect individual liberty," Hawley said in an interview. Without some limits imposed by the companies or by the government, he said, "we're going to have a huge problem with the invasion of basic rights and liberties."
The hearing is expected to feature a Florida woman who spent 13 days in jail after her car was spotted by a Flock camera a few miles from a fatal crash involving a similar vehicle.
Hawley said there may be an appetite in the Senate to pursue regulation.

Some police and public-safety officials say Flock, which has about 120,000 cameras nationwide, helps prevent and solve crime, including child abductions and hit-and-run crashes. But in a point of rare agreement between the left and the right, a national backlash has brewed over concerns that the cameras violate privacy and can be misused, with critics citing incidents where officers have allegedly used Flock's cameras for stalking.

Flock doesn't maintain a "single consolidated count of confirmed customer misuse," it said in the letter, and whether a user's searches were legitimate or resulted in disciplinary action is up to its customers.

The company rolled out a new system in April that flags unusual use. The company is also instituting a feature that will lock out users behaving abnormally. It has flagged multiple instances of misuse, including in some cases that led to arrests, the company said in its letter.

Flock recently changed its default data-retention period for new customers to seven days from 30 days. (Existing customers need to opt in to that change.) Customers can request a longer retention period but it must be approved "either by an elected governing body...or by an elected official," Flock wrote.
About 3% of its law-enforcement customers keep data for longer than 30 days, the company said, and the maximum allowable period is one year.
